questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. **IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**
Released Wednesday, October 14 · **Due Thursday, November 5, 6:00 PM Central** · 10% of course grade

Covers Lectures 6, 7 and 9: learned representations, training with early stopping, self-supervised pre-training, frozen representations, and fine-tuning.

## The situation

Kestrel Composites cures carbon-fibre panels for aircraft interiors. Every panel is cured in an instrumented autoclave that logs **160 process gauges**. Quality control is done by **destructive testing**: a panel is loaded to failure in a press and its interlaminar shear strength recorded.

Destructive testing is expensive. Each test costs about **$1,400 in lab time and destroys a $3,000 panel**. Over five years the lab has tested **2,000 panels**. Meanwhile every panel ever cured — **20,000 of them** — has a complete gauge trace sitting in the historian, unlabelled and unused.

Quality wants to predict strength from the gauges and test only the panels the model is unsure about. An engineer has fitted a regularized linear model on the 160 gauges. It is not accurate enough, and his read is that the fix is more data:

> "We're at 2,000 tested panels. The model is still well short of what the spec needs. My recommendation is to budget another 2,000 tests over the next two years and re-fit."

The Head of Quality wants a second opinion before signing off on **$8.8 million** of destroyed panels and lab time.

## The three questions

> 1. Will more destructive tests fix the current model?
> 2. Can the 20,000 unlabelled traces be made useful?
> 3. For the next panel family, how many destructive tests should Kestrel budget?

You are not trying to win a modelling competition. There are no marks for beating the models prescribed below.

---

## What Handout 9 gives you

Handout 9 establishes, with numbers, the results this assignment applies. You are not asked to rediscover them.

- **§2** — self-supervised pre-training: hide part of an input, ask a network to rebuild it, and you have a training signal that needs no labels.
- **§2.1** — the three ways to use the resulting encoder: freeze it and fit something simple on top, fine-tune it, or ignore it and train from scratch.
- **§3.1–3.2** — pre-training substitutes for labelled data, so its value is greatest where labels are scarcest and shrinks as they accumulate. The rule by label regime: freeze at tens of labels, fine-tune at hundreds to thousands, train from scratch at tens of thousands.
- **§3.3** — the control that is usually omitted: an untrained encoder of identical shape. Without it you cannot separate "pre-training learned something" from "this architecture makes useful random features."

Your job is to apply these to Kestrel's data and say what they imply for Kestrel's budget.

---

## The protocol

Fixed, and implemented in `starter/kestrel.py`. You should not need to change any of it.

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Label counts | *n* ∈ {50, 100, 250, 1000}, drawn from the 2,000 labelled panels |
| Label draws | **5 per cell**, from `label_subset(n, replicate)` |
| Pre-training seeds | **3** — pre-train three encoders, once each, and reuse them in every cell |
| Pre-training | Masked reconstruction: hide 30% of the gauges, rebuild them. 40 epochs, Adam at 3e-3 |
| Encoder | 160 → 64 → 16 → 160. The **representation is the first hidden layer**, 64 numbers |
| Frozen head | Ridge on those 64 numbers |
| Incumbent baseline | The same ridge, on the 160 raw gauges |
| From scratch | 160 → 64 → 1, Adam at 2e-3 |
| Fine-tuning | The same network started from the pre-trained encoder, Adam at 1e-3 |
| Early stopping | 25% inner validation split, patience 60, at most 800 epochs |
| Evaluation | `labeled_dev.csv` for everything in Part 1 |

**Why five label draws and three pre-training seeds.** Both are sources of variation and both are large here. With 50 labels the answer depends on *which* 50 panels happened to get tested, and a pre-trained encoder is itself a random object — two runs of the same pre-training produce different representations. At *n* = 50 the standard deviation across runs is bigger than several of the gaps you will be comparing. Report the standard deviation next to every mean, and do not read a difference smaller than it.

**What each cell averages over.** Use these run counts, so that every submission's table is comparable:

| Row | Runs per cell |
|---|---|
| Ridge on the raw gauges | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate` |
| Frozen encoder + ridge | 15 — each of the 3 encoders × 5 label draws |
| Frozen random encoder + ridge | 5 — one `random_encoder()` × 5 label draws |
| Network from scratch | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate` |
| Fine-tuned encoder | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate`, draw *r* starting from encoder *r* mod 3, so all three encoders are used |

**Pre-train once per seed, outside your label loop.** Pre-training is the only slow step, about 10 seconds. Nothing about it depends on the labels. Doing it inside the loop turns a two-minute analysis into an hour.

**Two evaluation extracts.** Everything you compare is scored on `labeled_dev.csv`. `labeled_test.csv` is scored once, on the single pipeline you recommend. Anything you decide by looking at data is decided on dev.

---

## Part 1 — One table

**Exhibit 1.** Five methods at four label counts, scored on the dev extract, each cell a mean and a standard deviation:

1. **Ridge on the 160 raw gauges** — the incumbent.
2. **Frozen encoder + ridge** — pre-train on the unlabelled traces, freeze, fit ridge on the representation.
3. **Frozen random encoder + ridge** — the control Handout 9 §3.3 requires.
4. **Network from scratch.**
5. **Fine-tuned encoder.**

`starter/kestrel.py` has one function for each. The whole table is two nested loops.

Then answer, in the memo:

1. **What happens to the incumbent as labels accumulate?** Compare its error at *n* = 50 against *n* = 1000, and against the error you would get by ignoring the gauges entirely and predicting the mean strength. Say what kind of limit this is — a shortage of data, or something else — and how your table tells the two apart.
2. **What does pre-training buy, and at which label counts?** Give the comparison against training from scratch at the same *n*.
3. **What does the random-encoder row rule out?** State what your table would have meant without it.
4. **Where does the ordering change?** Compare the frozen encoder against training from scratch at each label count. Say where the ordering changes, if it does, and where your standard deviations do not let you say. Bracket the crossover — four label counts bracket it, they do not locate it.

## Part 2 — The recommendation

**`memo.pdf` — at most 2 pages of prose plus Exhibit 1**, addressed to the Head of Quality. Answer her three questions in order:

1. **Will more destructive tests fix the current model?** Give the number that settles it.
2. **Can the unlabelled traces be made useful?** Say what method you would deploy at Kestrel's current label count, and what error it gives against the incumbent's.
3. **How many tests should the next panel family budget?** Give a number, and say what happens on either side of it. Convert it to money at $4,400 per tested panel, against the engineer's proposed 2,000.

Then score your recommended pipeline **once** on `labeled_test.csv`, report that number beside its dev counterpart, and note the difference in one sentence.

Close with what your evidence does not establish.

---

## Optional extension (up to 4 bonus points)

Not required, and a wrong answer cannot lower your score. Pick one.

- **Does the pretext task have to be hard?** `pretrain()` takes `mask_fraction`. Try 0.05 and 0.60 alongside the prescribed 0.30 and report what the frozen representation is worth in each case.
- **How much unlabelled data do you need?** Pre-train on the first 2,000 traces instead of all 20,000 and report the difference. Say what that implies for a plant that has just installed the instrumentation.
- **Beat the incumbent honestly.** The linear model fails for a structural reason. Construct a feature set that fixes it without any pre-training, fit the same ridge on it, and say how close it gets and what you had to know to build it. Keep the model a ridge: the point is the features, not a more flexible learner.

## How marks are typically lost

None of these is a trick. All are recoverable by re-reading the brief before you submit.

- **The table without the control.** Criterion 1 asks for a specific extra row and the brief says which handout section requires it. A table that omits it cannot support the claim it is being used to make, and cannot score above half marks here.
- **One pre-training run.** A pre-trained encoder is a random object; two runs of the same procedure give different representations. The protocol says three, and says to average.
- **Reading a difference smaller than its standard deviation.** At the smallest label count several rows overlap. Reporting an ordering the experiment cannot resolve is worse than reporting that it cannot resolve it.
- **Announcing a crossover to the decimal.** Four label counts bracket a crossover. They do not locate one.
- **Diagnosing the incumbent as short of data.** Criterion 2 asks what kind of limit it is hitting. The table contains the evidence that settles it; use it rather than asserting.
- **Explaining the incumbent's failure without reference to the process.** The data dictionary records what Process Engineering says about how strength arises. A good answer connects the shape of the failure to that description.
- **Selecting on the test extract.** Choosing the method or the label count by looking at it is a criterion 4 deduction even when the number is right. So is scoring several pipelines on it and reporting the best.
- **Pre-training inside the label loop.** Not a criterion by itself, but it is where nearly all the reported pain on this assignment comes from.
- **A memo that reports the study and never answers the question.** The Head of Quality asked whether to spend $8.8 million. An exhibit and no number is a criterion 3 failure regardless of how good the exhibits are.
- **A generic AI process note.** "Used AI to help write code, verified output" earns nothing under criterion 5.
# Kestrel Composites — data dictionary

Extract prepared by Process Engineering, September 2026.

**Grain.** One row per cured panel.

---

## The gauges (160 columns, identical in every file)

Every panel is cured in an autoclave instrumented with 160 gauges. All 160 are logged automatically for every panel, whether or not that panel is ever tested.

| Block | Columns | What it reads |
|---|---|---|
| Oven zone temperature | `cure_temp_z01` … `cure_temp_z40` | Thermocouples distributed through the oven, °C |
| Tool pressure | `press_p01` … `press_p32` | Pressure taps under the vacuum bag, kPa |
| Resin flow | `resin_flow_f01` … `resin_flow_f32` | Flow-front gauges around the tool, arbitrary units |
| Dielectric cure monitor | `dielectric_d01` … `dielectric_d32` | Ion-viscosity probes tracking the cure reaction |
| Vacuum line | `vacuum_v01` … `vacuum_v24` | Line pressures at the bag ports, kPa |

The gauges are **highly redundant**. They are 160 different views of a much smaller number of underlying process conditions — how hot the part actually got, how fast it got there, how completely the resin flowed, how much contamination was present. Two gauges on opposite sides of the same oven zone tell you nearly the same thing. This redundancy is why a gauge that drops out can be reconstructed from the others, and it is worth keeping in mind when you look at what pre-training does.

## The identifier and the target

| Column | Definition |
|---|---|
| `panel_id` | Panel identifier, unique across all four files. The prefix says which file a panel is in: `TR` train, `DV` dev, `TS` test, `UL` unlabelled. |
| `strength_mpa` | **Target.** Interlaminar shear strength, MPa. Measured by loading the panel to failure in a press. Present only in the three `labeled_*` files. |

Measuring it destroys the panel. That is the whole problem: a labelled row costs a saleable part plus about four hours of lab time, and an unlabelled row costs nothing at all.

**A note on negative values.** About 1–2% of labelled panels show a strength below zero, which no real panel can have. Like every dataset in this course, this extract is simulated, and those values come from the simulation's severe-contamination term rather than from a measurement. Leave them in: they are the badly delaminated panels, and the prescribed models and every comparison in the brief are computed with them included.

## What Process Engineering says about strength

> Strength needs two things to go right at once. The resin has to flow far enough to wet out every ply, and the cure has to run far enough to convert the matrix. A panel that is beautifully wetted but under-cured is weak. A panel that is fully cured but resin-starved is weak in a different way. **You cannot make up for a deficit in one with a surplus in the other** — the two failure modes multiply rather than add.
>
> Separately, contamination above a threshold causes delamination. Below the threshold it does nothing measurable; above it, strength falls away sharply.

That paragraph is a description of the physics, not a hint about modelling. It is here because it is what the process engineers would tell you, and it is relevant to at least one thing you will observe.

---

## The files

| File | Rows | Labelled | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `labeled_train.csv` | 2,000 | yes | fitting |
| `labeled_dev.csv` | 1,000 | yes | every comparison you make |
| `labeled_test.csv` | 1,000 | yes | scored once, at the end |
| `unlabeled_traces.csv.gz` | 20,000 | no | pre-training |

All four come from the same autoclave and the same period. No panel appears in more than one file. The unlabelled file is gzipped; `pandas.read_csv` opens it directly, and `starter/kestrel.py` already does.

`dev` and `test` are interchangeable except in what you are allowed to do with them: `dev` is where you compare things, `test` is scored once on whatever you end up recommending. They are not equally hard — `var(y)` is about 10% lower on `test` — so expect a small difference and report it rather than accounting for it.
# How to approach the assignments

**IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**
Read this once before Assignment 1, and re-read §5 before each submission.

---

## 1. What is being graded

You have a coding agent (`05_setting_up_your_agent.md`). It can write a modeling pipeline faster
than you can describe one, so writing the pipeline is not the skill being assessed.

What is assessed is the part that stays yours:

- deciding what question is actually being asked
- noticing when an answer is too good
- knowing what evidence would settle a disagreement
- saying what the evidence does and does not support

The broad goal of these assignments is to help you become comfortable working with AI to define and implement machine learning pipelines in a business context. To do that, you need a certain level of competency in the core concepts of machine learning. And imparting that competency is the broad goal of the course. 

Each assignment is preparation for an in-person exam where you will have none of these tools. If you
finish an assignment and could not explain your headline number on paper, it has not done its job.

---

## 2. What every assignment looks like

A business situation, a dataset, and **an analysis someone else has already done** — an analyst, a
contractor, an engineer. That analysis is plausible, arithmetically correct, but also wrong. Your task is
not "build a model." It is "understand what is wrong, why it is wrong, establish what is true, and say what should be done."

Four things are submitted every time:

| | |
|---|---|
| `memo.pdf` or `memo.md` | To a named business reader. Length limit stated per assignment, and enforced. |
| `analysis/` | Your code. Runs end to end from one command. |
| `ai_process_note.md` | One page. What you delegated, what you rejected, how you checked. |
| `sessions/` | Complete exported history of every AI session used. |

---

## 3. A working order that tends to go well

**Read the brief and the data dictionary yourself first.** The dictionaries record how each column
is produced and *when*. That timing information decides which columns you may use, and it is easier
to take in before a model exists to distract you.

**Write down what you expect before you compute anything.** What is the base rate? What order of
magnitude should the effect be? What would a suspiciously good result look like? Two minutes of this
is what makes you able to be surprised, and being surprised is how you find things.

**Get a baseline before you get a model.** Every assignment has a do-nothing answer — predict the
majority class, predict the mean, keep the current price. Compute it. It is the denominator for
everything that follows and the number most often missing from an agent's output.

**Change one thing at a time.** Where an assignment asks for an audit trail — one row per problem,
one fix, and the resulting number — build it as you go rather than reconstructing it at the end. It
is also your best defence against an agent that quietly fixed three things at once.

---

## 4. Working with your agent

The assignments are graded lightly, and in principle, you can delegate the majority of work to AI. However, this goes against the course's learning goals and will make you struggle in the in-person assessments. Hence, the following strategy is recommended for optimal learning.

**Delegate the work, not the judgment.** Good to hand over: "write a grouped cross-validation split
by member_id", "sweep the ridge penalty over the grid and plot train and validation error". Not good
to hand over: "tell me whether this model is good enough to deploy", "write the recommendation."
The second list is the assignment.

**Give it the business context, not just the file.** An agent told "predict churn from this CSV" will
optimise accuracy. An agent told what an offer costs and what a retained member is worth will do
something quite different. The context is in the brief; pass it along.

**Ask it to argue against itself.** "What would have to be true for this estimate to be wrong?" and
"What is the strongest objection to this conclusion?" are the two highest-yield prompts in the course.

**Be suspicious of agreement.** If the first answer confirms what you expected and nothing errored,
slow down rather than speed up.

**Do not let it choose the evaluation design.** Splits, metrics, units of analysis, and what counts as
held out are the graded content of this course. An agent will pick a sensible default, and these
datasets are built to punish sensible defaults.

**If you do not understand what it produced, stop.** Get it explained or throw it out. You are
responsible for every line and may be asked in class to explain any of it.

**Export your session before you close it** (`03_exporting_your_session_history.md`). The Codex app
copies to the clipboard rather than to a file, so paste it somewhere immediately.

---

## 5. The memo

Written to a named person who has a decision to make and will read the first paragraph carefully and
the rest quickly.

- **Lead with the recommendation.** Not the method, not the data cleaning.
- **Give the number, then the number it replaces.** "The honest estimate is X, not the Y in the
  current proposal, and the gap is mostly Z."
- **Quantify the uncertainty once, plainly, and move on.** A memo that never commits is not useful.
- **State conditions so someone could check them.** "Deploy if corporate accounts stay under 15% of
  the book" is a recommendation. "Deploy with caution" is not.
- **Respect the length limit.** Exhibits do not count against prose length; prose does.

---

## 6. Before you submit

Full list in `04_submission_checklist.md`. The five that matter most:

- [ ] The analysis runs end to end, from a clean copy of the folder, with one command.
- [ ] Every number in the memo comes from that run.
- [ ] Every session is exported into `sessions/`, complete and unedited.
- [ ] The process note names specific things you rejected or corrected. If you rejected nothing all
      assignment, think about that before writing it down.
- [ ] You can explain any part of the submission out loud, without notes.

That last item is not decorative. You may be asked to explain or modify a piece of your submitted
work in a short oral check.

1	# Assignment 2 — Learning a representation without labels
2	
3	**IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**
4	Released Wednesday, October 14 · **Due Thursday, November 5, 6:00 PM Central** · 10% of course grade
5	
6	Covers Lectures 6, 7 and 9: learned representations, training with early stopping, self-supervised pre-training, frozen representations, and fine-tuning.
7	
8	Expected effort: **4–6 focused hours**. The architectures, learning rates, sample sizes and splits are fixed for you below and implemented in `starter/kestrel.py`. You will not have to write a neural network or a training loop. Your work is to run one comparison, read it, and make a recommendation.
9	
10	Running the code needs only Lectures 6 and 7, which you have already had, so build the table in the first week. Lecture 9 on 22 October is what tells you how to read it, and Midterm 2 on 29 October covers the same material — so working through the table before the exam is good preparation for it. Handout 9 is posted with Lecture 9; until then, the summary under *What Handout 9 gives you* below is everything you need to build the table. The deadline falls a week after the exam so that you are not doing both in the same week.
11	
12	---
13	
14	## The situation
15	
16	Kestrel Composites cures carbon-fibre panels for aircraft interiors. Every panel is cured in an instrumented autoclave that logs **160 process gauges**. Quality control is done by **destructive testing**: a panel is loaded to failure in a press and its interlaminar shear strength recorded.
17	
18	Destructive testing is expensive. Each test costs about **$1,400 in lab time and destroys a $3,000 panel**. Over five years the lab has tested **2,000 panels**. Meanwhile every panel ever cured — **20,000 of them** — has a complete gauge trace sitting in the historian, unlabelled and unused.
19	
20	Quality wants to predict strength from the gauges and test only the panels the model is unsure about. An engineer has fitted a regularized linear model on the 160 gauges. It is not accurate enough, and his read is that the fix is more data:
21	
22	> "We're at 2,000 tested panels. The model is still well short of what the spec needs. My recommendation is to budget another 2,000 tests over the next two years and re-fit."
23	
24	The Head of Quality wants a second opinion before signing off on **$8.8 million** of destroyed panels and lab time.
25	
26	## The three questions
27	
28	> 1. Will more destructive tests fix the current model?
29	> 2. Can the 20,000 unlabelled traces be made useful?
30	> 3. For the next panel family, how many destructive tests should Kestrel budget?
31	
32	You are not trying to win a modelling competition. There are no marks for beating the models prescribed below.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## What Handout 9 gives you
37	
38	Handout 9 establishes, with numbers, the results this assignment applies. You are not asked to rediscover them.
39	
40	- **§2** — self-supervised pre-training: hide part of an input, ask a network to rebuild it, and you have a training signal that needs no labels.
41	- **§2.1** — the three ways to use the resulting encoder: freeze it and fit something simple on top, fine-tune it, or ignore it and train from scratch.
42	- **§3.1–3.2** — pre-training substitutes for labelled data, so its value is greatest where labels are scarcest and shrinks as they accumulate. The rule by label regime: freeze at tens of labels, fine-tune at hundreds to thousands, train from scratch at tens of thousands.
43	- **§3.3** — the control that is usually omitted: an untrained encoder of identical shape. Without it you cannot separate "pre-training learned something" from "this architecture makes useful random features."
44	
45	Your job is to apply these to Kestrel's data and say what they imply for Kestrel's budget.
46	
47	---
48	
49	## The protocol
50	
51	Fixed, and implemented in `starter/kestrel.py`. You should not need to change any of it.
52	
53	| | Value |
54	|---|---|
55	| Label counts | *n* ∈ {50, 100, 250, 1000}, drawn from the 2,000 labelled panels |
56	| Label draws | **5 per cell**, from `label_subset(n, replicate)` |
57	| Pre-training seeds | **3** — pre-train three encoders, once each, and reuse them in every cell |
58	| Pre-training | Masked reconstruction: hide 30% of the gauges, rebuild them. 40 epochs, Adam at 3e-3 |
59	| Encoder | 160 → 64 → 16 → 160. The **representation is the first hidden layer**, 64 numbers |
60	| Frozen head | Ridge on those 64 numbers |
61	| Incumbent baseline | The same ridge, on the 160 raw gauges |
62	| From scratch | 160 → 64 → 1, Adam at 2e-3 |
63	| Fine-tuning | The same network started from the pre-trained encoder, Adam at 1e-3 |
64	| Early stopping | 25% inner validation split, patience 60, at most 800 epochs |
65	| Evaluation | `labeled_dev.csv` for everything in Part 1 |
66	
67	**Why five label draws and three pre-training seeds.** Both are sources of variation and both are large here. With 50 labels the answer depends on *which* 50 panels happened to get tested, and a pre-trained encoder is itself a random object — two runs of the same pre-training produce different representations. At *n* = 50 the standard deviation across runs is bigger than several of the gaps you will be comparing. Report the standard deviation next to every mean, and do not read a difference smaller than it.
68	
69	**What each cell averages over.** Use these run counts, so that every submission's table is comparable:
70	
71	| Row | Runs per cell |
72	|---|---|
73	| Ridge on the raw gauges | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate` |
74	| Frozen encoder + ridge | 15 — each of the 3 encoders × 5 label draws |
75	| Frozen random encoder + ridge | 5 — one `random_encoder()` × 5 label draws |
76	| Network from scratch | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate` |
77	| Fine-tuned encoder | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate`, draw *r* starting from encoder *r* mod 3, so all three encoders are used |
78	
79	**Pre-train once per seed, outside your label loop.** Pre-training is the only slow step, about 10 seconds. Nothing about it depends on the labels. Doing it inside the loop turns a two-minute analysis into an hour.
80	
81	**Two evaluation extracts.** Everything you compare is scored on `labeled_dev.csv`. `labeled_test.csv` is scored once, on the single pipeline you recommend. Anything you decide by looking at data is decided on dev.

88	
89	1. **Ridge on the 160 raw gauges** — the incumbent.
90	2. **Frozen encoder + ridge** — pre-train on the unlabelled traces, freeze, fit ridge on the representation.
91	3. **Frozen random encoder + ridge** — the control Handout 9 §3.3 requires.
92	4. **Network from scratch.**
93	5. **Fine-tuned encoder.**

100	2. **What does pre-training buy, and at which label counts?** Give the comparison against training from scratch at the same *n*.
101	3. **What does the random-encoder row rule out?** State what your table would have meant without it.
102	4. **Where does the ordering change?** Compare the frozen encoder against training from scratch at each label count. Say where the ordering changes, if it does, and where your standard deviations do not let you say. Bracket the crossover — four label counts bracket it, they do not locate it.

104	## Part 2 — The recommendation
105	
106	**`memo.pdf` — at most 2 pages of prose plus Exhibit 1**, addressed to the Head of Quality. Answer her three questions in order:
107	
108	1. **Will more destructive tests fix the current model?** Give the number that settles it.
109	2. **Can the unlabelled traces be made useful?** Say what method you would deploy at Kestrel's current label count, and what error it gives against the incumbent's.
110	3. **How many tests should the next panel family budget?** Give a number, and say what happens on either side of it. Convert it to money at $4,400 per tested panel, against the engineer's proposed 2,000.

AI process note specific about what was delegated, what was rejected or corrected, and how the numbers were checked. | **10** |
186	| **Bonus** | **Optional extension.** One of the three, with the implication for the recommendation stated. Partial credit available; a wrong answer cannot lower your score. | **+4** |

192	## How marks are typically lost
193	
194	None of these is a trick. All are recoverable by re-reading the brief before you submit.
195	
196	- **The table without the control.** Criterion 1 asks for a specific extra row and the brief says which handout section requires it. A table that omits it cannot support the claim it is being used to make, and cannot score above half marks here.
197	- **One pre-training run.** A pre-trained encoder is a random object; two runs of the same procedure give different representations. The protocol says three, and says to average.
198	- **Reading a difference smaller than its standard deviation.** At the smallest label count several rows overlap. Reporting an ordering the experiment cannot resolve is worse than reporting that it cannot resolve it.
199	- **Announcing a crossover to the decimal.** Four label counts bracket a crossover. They do not locate one.
200	- **Diagnosing the incumbent as short of data.** Criterion 2 asks what kind of limit it is hitting. The table contains the evidence that settles it; use it rather than asserting.
201	- **Explaining the incumbent's failure without reference to the process.** The data dictionary records what Process Engineering says about how strength arises. A good answer connects the shape of the failure to that description.
202	- **Selecting on the test extract.** Choosing the method or the label count by looking at it is a criterion 4 deduction even when the number is right. So is scoring several pipelines on it and reporting the best.
203	- **Pre-training inside the label loop.** Not a criterion by itself, but it is where nearly all the reported pain on this assignment comes from.
204	- **A memo that reports the study and never answers the question.** The Head of Quality asked whether to spend $8.8 million. An exhibit and no number is a criterion 3 failure regardless of how good the exhibits are.
205	- **A generic AI process note.** "Used AI to help write code, verified output" earns nothing under criterion 5.
206	# Kestrel Composites — data dictionary
207	
208	Extract prepared by Process Engineering, September 2026.
209	
210	**Grain.** One row per cured panel.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## The gauges (160 columns, identical in every file)
215	
216	Every panel is cured in an autoclave instrumented with 160 gauges. All 160 are logged automatically for every panel, whether or not that panel is ever tested.
217	
218	| Block | Columns | What it reads |
219	|---|---|---|
220	| Oven zone temperature | `cure_temp_z01` … `cure_temp_z40` | Thermocouples distributed through the oven, °C |
221	| Tool pressure | `press_p01` … `press_p32` | Pressure taps under the vacuum bag, kPa |
222	| Resin flow | `resin_flow_f01` … `resin_flow_f32` | Flow-front gauges around the tool, arbitrary units |
223	| Dielectric cure monitor | `dielectric_d01` … `dielectric_d32` | Ion-viscosity probes tracking the cure reaction |
224	| Vacuum line | `vacuum_v01` … `vacuum_v24` | Line pressures at the bag ports, kPa |
225	
226	The gauges are **highly redundant**. They are 160 different views of a much smaller number of underlying process conditions — how hot the part actually got, how fast it got there, how completely the resin flowed, how much contamination was present. Two gauges on opposite sides of the same oven zone tell you nearly the same thing. This redundancy is why a gauge that drops out can be reconstructed from the others, and it is worth keeping in mind when you look at what pre-training does.
227	
228	## The identifier and the target
229	
230	| Column | Definition |
231	|---|---|
232	| `panel_id` | Panel identifier, unique across all four files. The prefix says which file a panel is in: `TR` train, `DV` dev, `TS` test, `UL` unlabelled. |
233	| `strength_mpa` | **Target.** Interlaminar shear strength, MPa. Measured by loading the panel to failure in a press. Present only in the three `labeled_*` files. |
234	
235	Measuring it destroys the panel. That is the whole problem: a labelled row costs a saleable part plus about four hours of lab time, and an unlabelled row costs nothing at all.
236	
237	**A note on negative values.** About 1–2% of labelled panels show a strength below zero, which no real panel can have. Like every dataset in this course, this extract is simulated, and those values come from the simulation's severe-contamination term rather than from a measurement. Leave them in: they are the badly delaminated panels, and the prescribed models and every comparison in the brief are computed with them included.
238	
239	## What Process Engineering says about strength
240	
241	> Strength needs two things to go right at once. The resin has to flow far enough to wet out every ply, and the cure has to run far enough to convert the matrix. A panel that is beautifully wetted but under-cured is weak. A panel that is fully cured but resin-starved is weak in a different way. **You cannot make up for a deficit in one with a surplus in the other** — the two failure modes multiply rather than add.
242	>
243	> Separately, contamination above a threshold causes delamination. Below the threshold it does nothing measurable; above it, strength falls away sharply.
244	
245	That paragraph is a description of the physics, not a hint about modelling. It is here because it is what the process engineers would tell you, and it is relevant to at least one thing you will observe.
246	
247	---
248	
249	## The files
250	
251	| File | Rows | Labelled | Use |
252	|---|---|---|---|
253	| `labeled_train.csv` | 2,000 | yes | fitting |
254	| `labeled_dev.csv` | 1,000 | yes | every comparison you make |
255	| `labeled_test.csv` | 1,000 | yes | scored once, at the end |
256	| `unlabeled_traces.csv.gz` | 20,000 | no | pre-training |
257	
258	All four come from the same autoclave and the same period. No panel appears in more than one file. The unlabelled file is gzipped; `pandas.read_csv` opens it directly, and `starter/kestrel.py` already does.
259	
260	`dev` and `test` are interchangeable except in what you are allowed to do with them: `dev` is where you compare things, `test` is scored once on whatever you end up recommending. They are not equally hard — `var(y)` is about 10% lower on `test` — so expect a small difference and report it rather than accounting for it.

304	## 3. A working order that tends to go well
305	
306	**Read the brief and the data dictionary yourself first.** The dictionaries record how each column
307	is produced and *when*. That timing information decides which columns you may use, and it is easier
308	to take in before a model exists to distract you.
309	
310	**Write down what you expect before you compute anything.** What is the base rate? What order of
311	magnitude should the effect be? What would a suspiciously good result look like? Two minutes of this
312	is what makes you able to be surprised, and being surprised is how you find things.
313	
314	**Get a baseline before you get a model.** Every assignment has a do-nothing answer — predict the
315	majority class, predict the mean, keep the current price. Compute it. It is the denominator for
316	everything that follows and the number most often missing from an agent's output.
317	
318	**Change one thing at a time.** Where an assignment asks for an audit trail — one row per problem,
319	one fix, and the resulting number — build it as you go rather than reconstructing it at the end. It
320	is also your best defence against an agent that quietly fixed three things at once.

324	## 4. Working with your agent
325	
326	The assignments are graded lightly, and in principle, you can delegate the majority of work to AI. However, this goes against the course's learning goals and will make you struggle in the in-person assessments. Hence, the following strategy is recommended for optimal learning.
327	
328	**Delegate the work, not the judgment.** Good to hand over: "write a grouped cross-validation split
329	by member_id", "sweep the ridge penalty over the grid and plot train and validation error". Not good
330	to hand over: "tell me whether this model is good enough to deploy", "write the recommendation."
331	The second list is the assignment.
332	
333	**Give it the business context, not just the file.** An agent told "predict churn from this CSV" will
334	optimise accuracy. An agent told what an offer costs and what a retained member is worth will do
335	something quite different. The context is in the brief; pass it along.
336	
337	**Ask it to argue against itself.** "What would have to be true for this estimate to be wrong?" and
338	"What is the strongest objection to this conclusion?" are the two highest-yield prompts in the course.

340	**Be suspicious of agreement.** If the first answer confirms what you expected and nothing errored,
341	slow down rather than speed up.

343	**Do not let it choose the evaluation design.** Splits, metrics, units of analysis, and what counts as
344	held out are the graded content of this course. An agent will pick a sensible default, and these
345	datasets are built to punish sensible defaults.

347	**If you do not understand what it produced, stop.** Get it explained or throw it out. You are
